sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source encompasses the southern and central portion of the Scicli Fault Zone in the Hyblean Plateau. This high angle, N-S-oriented, 70+ km-long shear zone extends from the Hyblean foreland area to the inflected foreland buried below the Gela-Catania foredeep deposits and the frontal part of the Apennines-Maghrebides orogenic wedge.
The Scicli Fault Zone is a long-lasting structure displaying a strong morphological and structural overprint from an older tectonic phase indicating right-lateral displacement along the shear zone. Conversely, geological evidence for the present activity is faint and is given primarily by displaced river courses and marine terraces, all indicating present-day left-lateral motion along the shear zone.
This fault zone is composed of four main N-S-to N10Â°-oriented segments, both west and east facing, extending from Palagonia (to the north) to Cava d'Aliga (to the south), near the coastline (Catalano et al., 2008). The overall geometry of the shear zone and the distribution of restraining and releasing bends in the overlap zones supply evidence for long-lived dextral shear. The main strike-slip faults are accompanied by secondary synthetic and antithetic faults, folds and joint sets, altogether suggesting right-lateral slip (e.g., Ghisetti and Vezzani, 1980).
Based on offset drainage patterns Catalano et al. (2008b) estimated a right-lateral displacement of ca. 2,000 m along the central part of this fault system. This offset was attained between 1.2-1.5 and 0.85 Ma, when its causative stress regime came to an end.
Displaced geomorphic markers such as diverted rivers and deformed marine terraces also constrain the style and rate of the most recent deformation. Near the coast, several fault strands of the Cava d'Aliga segment displace late Quaternary marine terraces (Grasso and Reuther, 1988) and the drainage network with a total sinistral offset of ca. 150 m and a vertical offset of ca. 10 m, yielding a slip rate of about 1.2 mm/a (Catalano et al., 2008). To the north, the drainage network crossing the Scicli Fault Zone near Ragusa and Giarratana displays a total left-lateral offset of about 1,250 m, which translates into an average late Quaternary slip rate in the order of 1.4 mm/a (Catalano et al., 2008).
The Scicli Fault Zone is the most prominent structural element of the Hyblean Plateau. According to the literature, the morphology of this elevated region is delineated by large normal fault systems that separate it from the Gela-Catania foredeep to the west and northwest, and from the Ionian basin to the east. To the north the Hyblean Plateau is paralleled by a NE-trending depression commonly referred to as Scordia-Lentini graben.
Geological observations, the present-day stress field and GPS data from a network stretching between the Hyblean Plateau and Mt. Etna, altogether indicate that this region is currently undergoing NNW-directed active shortening.
Musumeci et al. (2005) showed that NNE-SSW and NE-SW left-lateral strike-slip faulting mechanisms are common in the western and central portions of the Hyblean Plateau, suggesting such kinematics along the Scicli Fault Zone in agreement with observations on recent geologic and geomorphic displaced features.
Historical and instrumental catalogues (Boschi et al., 2000; Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2006; Guidoboni et al., 2007) show significant seismicity concentrated mainly near the northern margin of the Hyblean Plateau. The most important earthquakes that occurred in this area are the 4 February 1169 (Mw 6.6), the 10 December 1542 (Mw 6.6) and the 11 January 1693 (Mw 7.4) events (all magnitudes from Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004).
Two Individual Sources have been associated with the 11 January 1693 earthquake, the largest event listed in the Italian earthquake catalogue. The mainshock of the 1693 earthquake is likely to have included two or more subevents, as suggested by the existence of two separate concentrations of higher damage, but this hypothesis is not explicitly backed up by the available historical sources. The 1693 earthquake was preceded by a strong foreshock on 9 January (Mw 6.2, Imax VIII-IX) and by another foreshock on the same day. The 9 January event caused severe damage over the entire Hyblean Plateau and increased the vulnerability of the buildings, thus contributing to the very large damage caused on 11 January by the mainshock. Based on modeling of the intensity pattern using the Kinematic Function approach, Sirovich and Pettenati (2001) proposed a NNE-oriented, 60 km long-source characterized by oblique motion and nearly overlapping the Scicli Fault Zone.
In contrast, the 1169 and the 1542 earthquakes are not associated with any Individual Seismogenic Source.
The strike of this Source was based on the general orientation of mapped tectonic structures. The dip was based on field structural evidence. The rake was assumed to be representative of a dominant left-lateral component of motion, based on general geodynamic considerations, field structural data and geomorphic evidence. The minimum and maximum depth were based on geometrical considerations concerning the thickness of the seismogenic layer. The slip rate was based on geological data.
